teaser: More than two hundred children, some eighty games, and hardly a grown-up in sight.
review_notes:
Counts vary by scholar: about 80 games (often 83 or 91) and more than 200 children (often 230 to 250).
Size about 118 x 161 cm.
The adult-like faces and the 'folly' reading are standard interpretations, presented as readings, not facts.
The building is often compared to a town hall; presented as a reading.
A very few adults are sometimes identified (e.g. a woman throwing water from a window); the lesson says 'hardly any'.

lesson.text: A hoop is rolling. The boy in red tights has just struck it and his stick is still raised. Next to him a girl's hoop wobbles along. Behind them a child has been caught at the top of a leapfrog jump, and another hangs upside down from a rail. In one second all of them will have moved.

Bruegel stops the clock on an entire town at that instant. Nobody is posing, and nobody is looking at you. It is 1560, about three centuries before the camera, and he has painted what a snapshot would catch: hundreds of small bodies in the middle of doing something.

spots.title: Two hoops
spots.text: Barrel hoops driven with sticks, one by a boy, one by a girl. The circles are drawn so thinly you can see the ground through them.

spots.title: Leapfrog
spots.text: One child is in mid-air above a bent back, legs spread. To the right the next pair is already lining up.

spots.title: The barrel
spots.text: Two boys try to ride a big barrel lying on its side. One has a firm seat. The other is working out how to get on.

spots.title: The rail
spots.text: On a wooden bar in front of the big building, children hang and swing upside down, shirts falling over their heads.

lesson.text: You know every one of those games. That is the first surprise of this picture: how little has changed. Hoops, leapfrog, stilts, spinning tops, piggyback, tag, hobby horses, headstands. Scholars count around eighty different games in all, played by more than two hundred children.

One game is played with real bones. The two girls sitting on the ground at bottom left are tossing knucklebones, small ankle bones of sheep, the ancestor of the game of jacks. A few steps away a child holds a pig's bladder blown up like a balloon.

The second surprise is who is missing. This is a real-looking Flemish town, with a square, a stream and a long shopping street, and it has been handed over to the children. Hardly any adult is anywhere. To fit them all in, Bruegel had to bend space.
Two tricks let him show everything at once.

lines.label: A horizon near the top
lines.text: The skyline sits at the very top edge. You look steeply down, as from an upstairs window, so the ground tilts up like a table and no child hides another.

lines.label: The long street
lines.text: On the right a street shoots away toward a distant spire, with games going on all the way down it. It hints that the playing never ends, even beyond the frame.

lines.label: The fence
lines.text: The red fence is nearly the only bright, straight thing in the foreground. It gives the eye a place to rest, and of course somebody is riding it.

lesson.text: With that tilted ground, the panel reads almost like a page. It is oil on wood, about 118 by 161 cm (46 by 63 inches), and each figure is only a few centimeters tall. There is no hero and no center. Bruegel used the same bird's-eye layout a year earlier for a village full of proverbs.
The picture works as a catalog: one town, one moment, every game he could think of. It is among the first paintings in Europe to take childhood itself as a subject worth a large panel.

Is it only a catalog, though? Go near any face. The children are stocky, with round, serious heads. They wear smaller versions of adult clothes, as real children did then, and almost none of them is smiling. They play the way grown-ups work.
One child is not playing in the street. He leans out of a window with a big, grinning false face. Where?

spots.title: The mask
spots.text: At the window of the red house on the far left, a child holds a large mask over the sill to scare whoever passes below. Pretending to be somebody else is a game too.

lesson.text: That mask has encouraged a darker reading. In Bruegel's time, writers often compared adults chasing money or rank to children absorbed in games. Seen that way, the big building in the middle, which looks like a town hall, makes a sharp joke: the seat of serious business, overrun by players.

No one knows who ordered the painting or where it first hung. It surfaces in writing only in 1604, when the biographer Karel van Mander mentions a picture by Bruegel with “all manner of children's games”.

So which is it: a loving inventory of play, or a picture of humanity as overgrown children? Bruegel left no note, and the painting supports both. Wander through it yourself and see which reading the children talk you into.

spots.title: Stilts
spots.text: A figure on tall stilts towers against the wall of the big building, taller than its doorway.

spots.title: Knucklebones
spots.text: Two girls crouch over a handful of small bones. One has just thrown and the other watches the fall.

spots.title: Spinning skirts
spots.text: On the grass near the stream, girls whirl until their red skirts fill with air, then drop to the ground so the cloth settles in a perfect circle.

spots.title: Hobby horse
spots.text: A boy rides a stick with a horse's head, whip in hand. A toy this simple has changed very little since.

spots.title: The procession
spots.text: Children wrapped in blue and red cloaks walk in a solemn line. They are playing at a grown-up ceremony, most likely a baptism.

spots.title: The stream
spots.text: In the cool green corner at top left, children swim and paddle. It is the only quiet part of the picture.

spots.title: Tops
spots.text: Under the arches of the building, children whip spinning tops across the paving to keep them turning.

spots.title: The bladder
spots.text: A child holds an inflated pig's bladder with both arms, the balloon of the 1500s.

quiz.question: About how many different games do scholars count in the painting?
quiz.explanation: Some eighty games are played by more than two hundred children.

quiz.question: Why can you see every child clearly?
options: The horizon is very high, so you look steeply down
Bruegel painted only one row of figures
The children are all the same size as the houses
quiz.explanation: The high viewpoint tilts the ground up like a table.

quiz.question: What are knucklebones?
options: Small sheep bones tossed in a game like jacks
quiz.explanation: The girls at bottom left play with ankle bones of sheep.

quiz.question: What darker meaning have some viewers found in the picture?
options: That the town was struck by plague
That children should be at work
That adults pursuing their affairs are like children at play
quiz.explanation: Writers of the time compared grown-up ambitions to children's games.

quiz.question: What does the child at the far-left window hold?
quiz.explanation: He leans out with a big false face to scare passers-by.

facts.text: The town in the painting is full of adults supervising the games.
facts.explanation: Hardly any adult appears; the town belongs to the children.

facts.text: The children wear smaller versions of adult clothing.
facts.explanation: That is how real children were dressed in the 1500s.

facts.text: We know exactly who commissioned the painting.
facts.explanation: Its first owner is unknown; it is first mentioned in writing in 1604.
